original_question: For subgraph centrality SC(i, beta) = [e^(beta A)]_ii, say that two vertices interlace at beta when SC(i, beta) = SC(j, beta). Given k in N, characterize the smallest graph or graphs that contain a pair of vertices with at least k interlacing values of subgraph centrality. Conversely, for a graph with n vertices, determine the largest possible number of interlacing values for a pair of vertices, decide whether there are graph classes for which the following bound is attained: if A has d distinct eigenvalues, then any two non-cospectral vertices have at most d - 1 interlacing values of subgraph centrality, and find simple constructions of graphs with many interlacing values.
target_in_paper: Section 3, Problem 2, together with the immediately following informal sentence about constructing graphs with many interlacing values.
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper’s actual target. It correctly uses the paper’s subgraph-centrality notation SC(i,β) = [e^{βA}]_{ii}, correctly identifies interlacing as equality of two vertex subgraph centralities at a parameter value β, and it reproduces the three substantive parts of Section 3, Problem 2 almost verbatim: (i) for each k, find the smallest graph(s) with a pair of vertices having at least k interlacing values; (ii) for fixed n, maximize the number of interlacing values for a pair of vertices; and (iii) ask whether the d-1 upper bound can be attained. Your final clause about simple constructions also matches the paper’s immediately following informal related question.
missing_details: The paper’s default ambient setting here is a simple undirected graph G with real symmetric adjacency matrix A; weighted/directed/signed variants are discussed separately later, and allowing them changes the problem qualitatively.
The parameter β is restricted to positive real numbers.
By Definition 2.6, interlacing is defined for two non-cospectral vertices i and j; this exclusion matters because cospectral vertices agree for all β and would trivialize the counting problem.
Interlacing values are equivalently the positive zeros of g_{ij}(β) = [e^{βA}]_{ii} - [e^{βA}]_{jj}; for non-cospectral vertices this zero set is discrete.
The quantity d in the bound d-1 is the number of distinct eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix A, exactly as in Theorem 2.9.

To make 'smallest graph(s)' stand alone, one should say smallest by order, i.e. by number of vertices; that is the meaning suggested by the surrounding brute-force search over all small graphs with n ≤ 10.

The paper’s numbered Problem 2 ends with the attainment question for the bound d-1; the request for a simple construction of graphs with many interlacing values is stated separately as a related, more informal problem.
refined_question: Let G be a simple undirected graph with adjacency matrix A, and for β > 0 define the (exponential) subgraph centrality of vertex i by SC(i,β) = [e^{βA}]_{ii}. For two non-cospectral vertices i and j, call β an interlacing value if SC(i,β) = SC(j,β). Given k ∈ N, characterize the smallest graph(s), by number of vertices, that contain a pair of vertices with at least k interlacing values of subgraph centrality. Conversely, for an n-vertex graph, determine the largest possible number of interlacing values for a pair of vertices, and in particular decide whether there exist classes of graphs for which the general upper bound d-1 is attained, where d is the number of distinct eigenvalues of A.
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, for non-cospectral vertices i and j in a simple undirected graph G, study the positive zeros of g_{ij}(β) = [e^{βA}]_{ii} - [e^{βA}]_{jj}: given k ∈ N, characterize the smallest graph(s) for which g_{ij} has at least k positive zeros for some pair i,j; for fixed n, maximize the number of positive zeros of g_{ij}; and determine whether the upper bound d-1 from Theorem 2.9 can be attained.
justification: The draft clearly targets Section 3, Problem 2 (p. 16), not the earlier conjectural material: the wording 'Given k ∈ N, characterize the smallest graph(s)... Conversely... what is the largest number... In particular, are there classes of graphs for which the bound d−1 is attained?' is essentially the paper’s Problem 2 verbatim. The nearby sentence 'is there a simple way to construct graphs with many interlacing values?' explains your last clause, but it is presented by the paper as a separate informal add-on rather than part of the numbered problem. To make the question fully stand-alone and faithful to the paper, one must import the default setup from Section 2.1 (simple undirected graph; adjacency matrix A; β > 0; SC(i,β) = [e^{βA}]_{ii}), the precise Definition 2.6 of interlacing for non-cospectral vertices, and the fact that interlacing values are the zeros of g(β). The bound d−1 comes from Theorem 2.9, while Proposition 2.13 gives the sharper sign-change version that the paper mentions as context but does not substitute for Problem 2.
